frames.narration: The home screen needs 12 small requests. The naive client asks for them one by one. Each request has to wait for the one before, and for the screen to render its answer.
The link loses an attempt. The client does not know it was lost until its fixed 1,000 ms timeout fires, and then retries at once. That is waiting time, with the radio awake for nothing.
Between requests the client renders for a second or more. The radio goes quiet and has to wake up again for every request: 12 wake-ups, 15 requests, usable after 6,780 ms.
A better client sends all 12 requests together, with a timeout that follows the round trip. A lost one is retried after a growing, randomised pause, and the whole client has a retry budget.
Or it sends one batched request for the whole screen: one round trip, one wake-up, 540 ms. A bigger reply is hit harder by loss, so batches stay small and the server can return partial results.
A write times out after the server applied it. The client retries with the same idempotency key, and the server returns the first result instead of doing it twice.

An outage ends and 10,000 phones reconnect at the same second. With the same retry schedule on every phone, the server sees 10,000 requests per second, rejects 20,000 over the next seconds, and takes 15 s to serve everyone.
With jitter on the reconnect and on every retry, the phones spread over 10 seconds: a peak of 1,035 requests per second, none rejected. The same fleet, with randomness added.
